stances.claim: Franklin M. Drilon should have been President of the Republic of the Philippines -- among all the politicians of his time, he was the most qualified, most experienced, most effective, and most trustworthy, patriotic, sharp, humble, outspoken, pro-poor, unblemished by any scandal, and as a national politician has never lost an election (topped senatorial polls more than once, Senate President several times, Senate Minority Leader a few times).

Competent, prudent and collegial, Drilon knew how to think, act and work when leading the majority and how to fiscalize the majority, defend the national will and protect the marginalized when heading the minority.

CJP tried his best to inveigle Drilon to aspire for the presidency, sure that retiring popular President Aquino III would support him -- with either Mar Roxas or Grace Poe as his VP teammate in 2016, Drilon would have been unbeatable; in fact, Rodrigo Roa Duterte would not have run had he known Drilon would be the top contender. CJP pleaded motherland, patriotism, common welfare, and assured victory, but could not budge the distinguished former Senate President.

When the 2012 CJ vacancy opened due to Corona's impeachment removal, CJP asked Drilon to consider being the replacement, hounding him daily with personal meetings -- and after Drilon 'escaped' to San Francisco to avoid CJP, CJP still called him daily; Drilon promised on his return to go direct from NAIA to CJP's home to discuss with finality his refusal.

By Drilon's incorrigible refusal, he created a crisis in the Supreme Court because Aquino III did not want to appoint any incumbent senior associate justices named there by his predecessor Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo -- the incumbent justices signaled they would not object to Drilon as the first outsider Chief since the Court was founded in 1901 (only exception being Speaker Jose Yulo as CJ during World War 2). Given his impeccable legal track record and near-70 retirement age, Drilon would serve only a few years, giving the senior justices an opportunity to become Chief soon enough.
stances.rhetorical_move: incorrigible-refusal critique + first-outsider-since-1901 + Yulo-WW2 precedent anchoring

stances.claim: Because of his steadfast refusal, Aquino III appointed Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno, a very junior member who had served only two years (2010-2012) as associate justice and was ranked among the last third of the 15 justices; for this and other reasons CJP will no longer discuss, Sereno was ousted by her colleagues voting 8-6 via quo warranto -- not by the constitutional process of impeachment -- due to her failure to file some of her annual SALN while a UP law faculty member.
CJP will not preempt Frank and leaves it to him to explain to his readers and admirers in his Memoirs why he steadfastly declined to be President and/or Chief Justice.

Frank's first wife Violy Calvo fully and absolutely supported his political career -- CJP ventures she was not merely the wind beneath his sails but the driving force, the 'activist' who inspired and helped catapult him to his meteoric political career; CJP personally knew the lovely, kind and candid Violy, an upcoming NUSP leader CJP had founded and headed earlier on. Before she died of incurable illness, Violy helped choose Frank's new wife Mila Serrano Genuino -- a widow Violy knew would fit Frank's career and take care of him, as indeed she did and still does, 'lovingly, tenderly, eternally.'

More than this earthly life, Mila has uncannily and invisibly led Frank to imitate the Lord Jesus, whom Frank has proclaimed (like many of us) as his Lord and Master and vowed to imitate Him and join Him in Heaven one day. Though now retired from active politics, as he writes his Memoirs, Franklin M. Drilon remains a legend for what he has done and continues to do for our country and people -- he can rightly claim, as St. Paul did, that 'I have done my best. I have finished the race. I have kept the faith.'

one_paragraph_summary: Written as Drilon launched his autobiography 'Being Frank, a Memoir,' Panganiban reproduces the Foreword he authored, arguing that Drilon should have been President of the Republic -- the most qualified, experienced, effective, and trustworthy politician of his time. He recounts his unsuccessful pleas for Drilon to run in 2016 with Roxas or Poe (positing that Duterte would not have entered the race) and his daily lobbying in 2012 for Drilon to fill the post-Corona Chief Justice vacancy, including Drilon's escape to San Francisco and post-flight detour directly from NAIA to CJP's home to deliver his final refusal. The refusals led Aquino III to bypass Arroyo-appointed senior justices and name Sereno, who was later ousted 8-6 via quo warranto over unfiled SALNs. He closes warmly on Drilon's first wife Violy Calvo (the 'wind beneath his sails' and 'activist' driving force from NUSP days), her selection of Mila Genuino as his future second wife before her own death, and Drilon's St. Paul-quoting faith legacy.
